t:
(a) In General.—It is the policy of the United States that—
        (1) it is in the national interest for the Department, State departments of transportation, transit agencies, and all other recipients of Federal transportation funds—
            (A) to accelerate project delivery and reduce costs; and 
            (B) to ensure that the planning, design, engineering, construction, and financing of transportation projects is done in an efficient and effective manner, promoting accountability for public investments and encouraging greater private sector involvement in project financing and delivery while enhancing safety and protecting the environment;  
        (2) delay in the delivery of transportation projects increases project costs, harms the economy of the United States, and impedes the travel of the people of the United States and the shipment of goods for the conduct of commerce; and 
        (3) the Secretary shall identify and promote the deployment of innovation aimed at reducing the time and money required to deliver transportation projects while enhancing safety and protecting the environment.  
    (b) Project Delivery Initiative.—
        (1) In general.—To advance the policy described in subsection (a), the Secretary shall carry out a project delivery initiative under this section. 
        (2) Purposes.—The purposes of the project delivery initiative shall be—
            (A) to develop and advance the use of best practices to accelerate project delivery and reduce costs across all modes of transportation and expedite the deployment of technology and innovation; 
            (B) to implement provisions of law designed to accelerate project delivery; and 
            (C) to select eligible projects for applying experimental features to test innovative project delivery techniques.  
        (3) Advancing the use of best practices.—
            (A) In general.—In carrying out the initiative under this section, the Secretary shall identify and advance best practices to reduce delivery time and project costs, from planning through construction, for transportation projects and programs of projects regardless of mode and project size. 
            (B) Administration.—To advance the use of best practices, the Secretary shall—
                (i) engage interested parties, affected communities, resource agencies, and other stakeholders to gather information regarding opportunities for accelerating project delivery and reducing costs; 
                (ii) establish a clearinghouse for the collection, documentation, and advancement of existing and new innovative approaches and best practices; 
                (iii) disseminate information through a variety of means to transportation stakeholders on new innovative approaches and best practices; and 
                (iv) provide technical assistance to assist transportation stakeholders in the use of flexibility authority to resolve project delays and accelerate project delivery if feasible.   
        (4) Implementation of accelerated project delivery.—The Secretary shall ensure that the provisions of this subtitle designed to accelerate project delivery are fully implemented, including—
            (A) expanding eligibility of early acquisition of property prior to completion of environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (42 U.S.C. 4321 et seq.); 
            (B) allowing the use of the construction manager or general contractor method of contracting in the Federal-aid highway system; and 
            (C) establishing a demonstration program to streamline the relocation process by permitting a lump-sum payment for acquisition and relocation if elected by the displaced occupant.   
    (c) Expedited Project Delivery.—Section 101(b) of title 23, United States Code, is amended by adding at the end the following:“(4) Expedited project delivery.—“(A) In general.—Congress declares that it is in the national interest to expedite the delivery of surface transportation projects by substantially reducing the average length of the environmental review process.“(B) Policy of the united states.—Accordingly, it is the policy of the United States that—“(i) the Secretary shall have the lead role among Federal agencies in carrying out the environmental review process for surface transportation projects;“(ii) each Federal agency shall cooperate with the Secretary to expedite the environmental review process for surface transportation projects;“(iii) project sponsors shall not be prohibited from carrying out preconstruction project development activities concurrently with the environmental review process;“(iv) programmatic approaches shall be used to reduce the need for project-by-project reviews and decisions by Federal agencies; and“(v) the Secretary shall identify opportunities for project sponsors to assume responsibilities of the Secretary where such responsibilities can be assumed in a manner that protects public health, the environment, and public participation.”.

fable.w: The Secretary must engage interested parties, affected communities and other stakeholders, who are outside the federal government, to inform which best practices the federal project delivery initiative identifies and advances. The tempting "No" reading treats this as mere information-gathering like a study, or dismisses the section because the inter-agency cooperation language and the closing phrase "public participation" are only intra-government or boilerplate. Those parts would not qualify on their own, but the mandatory stakeholder engagement feeds a federal choice about what practices to promote, so it crosses the federal boundary.
fable.s: engage interested parties, affected communities, resource agencies, and other stakeholders to gather information regarding opportunities for accelerating project delivery and reducing costs

qwen_block.w: The section explicitly requires the Secretary to 'engage interested parties, affected communities, resource agencies, and other stakeholders' to gather information. These groups are outside the federal government, and their engagement constitutes participation in the decision-making process regarding project delivery practices. This fits the definition of consultation or coordination with outside entities.
qwen_block.s: (i) engage interested parties, affected communities, resource agencies, and other stakeholders to gather information regarding opportunities for accelerating project delivery and reducing costs;

opus.w: The Secretary must engage outside stakeholders, including interested parties and affected communities, to gather input. That input feeds the federal decision about which best practices to identify and advance under the project delivery initiative. This brings non-federal actors into federal decision-making. The other references (cooperation between agencies, 'public participation' named as a value, private sector involvement in financing) would not count on their own, but this engagement requirement does.
opus.s: (i) engage interested parties, affected communities, resource agencies, and other stakeholders to gather information regarding opportunities for accelerating project delivery and reducing costs;
opus.b:
I labelled this **Yes**, with moderate confidence (0.7).

**The tempting reading is wrong.** Much of the section looks like participation but isn't:
- Subsection (a) states policy goals and only mentions "greater private sector involvement in project financing."
- The amendment in subsection (c) is about cooperation between federal agencies.
- The phrase "public participation" in (c) only names a value to protect; it creates no process.

**What makes it Yes.** Subsection (b)(3)(B)(i) requires the Secretary to "engage interested parties, affected communities, resource agencies, and other stakeholders." Many of these are outside the federal government. The engagement feeds the Secretary's job of identifying and advancing best practices for delivering projects, which is a federal decision.

**Why I'm not more confident.** This differs from Example 3, where outside experts only shaped the contents of a study. Here, outside parties shape a program decision: which best practices the Secretary will identify and advance. That line is close, so the call could reasonably go the other way.

qwen_chat.w: The section requires the Secretary to engage stakeholders to 'gather information' for the purpose of identifying best practices. This is analogous to the Navy study example where consultation with experts was for the purpose of conducting a study/report, not for consultation on a specific federal decision. Gathering general information or best practices does not constitute the required consultation or coordination before a specific federal decision.
qwen_chat.s: (i) engage interested parties, affected communities, resource agencies, and other stakeholders to gather information regarding opportunities for accelerating project delivery and reducing costs;
qwen_chat.b:
Temptation: It looks like participation because it refers to engaging "interested parties, affected communities, resource agencies, and other stakeholders" to gather information.
Resolution: The engagement is for the purpose of gathering information to identify best practices, not for consultation or coordination on a specific federal decision. The definition requires consultation or coordination *before making a decision*. Gathering general information or best practices is not the same as participating in a specific decision-making process. Furthermore, the text mentions "public participation" in subsection (c)(v) but only in the context of protecting it, not requiring it as a specific procedural step in this section. The primary action described is the Secretary identifying and advancing best practices.

Wait, let's re-read carefully.
Subsection (b)(3)(B)(i): "engage interested parties, affected communities, resource agencies, and other stakeholders to gather information regarding opportunities for accelerating project delivery and reducing costs".
Is this "consultation or coordination... before making a decision"?
The decision being made is "identify and advance best practices". The engagement is to "gather information".
The definition says: "Participation is when the federal government may or must consult or coordinate with people outside of the government before making a decision."
Does gathering information count as consultation? Usually, "consultation" implies a two-way dialogue where the outside party's input influences the decision. "Gathering information" can be one-way.
However, "engage... stakeholders" often implies a form of consultation.
Let's look at the "No" traps: "reports to... Congress", "consultation BETWEEN federal agencies", "applications".
This is not a report to Congress. It is not intra-agency. It is not an application.
Is it "consultation"? The text says "engage... to gather information".
Compare to Example 2 (Estuary): "consultation and coordination with appropriate State and local governmental agencies... may allow a nongovernmental organization to serve as the non-Federal interest". That was a Yes.
Compare to Example 3 (Navy Study): "consultation with financial experts independent of the Department... Financial analysis associated with the report". That was a No because it was about the contents of a study/report, not a decision.
Here, the Secretary is carrying out an "initiative" to "identify and advance best practices". The engagement is to "gather information". This feels more like the Navy study (gathering info for a report/initiative) than the Estuary case (consultation before allowing a specific project/organization).
However, "affected communities" and "stakeholders" are outside parties.
Let's look at subsection (c)(v): "protects public health, the environment, and public participation." This mentions public participation but doesn't require it.

Let's look at the "Yes" criteria again:
- requiring a public comment period
- public hearing/meeting
- advisory committee with non-federal members
- consultation/coordination with states/tribes/locals/outside entities *before a federal action*
- right to sue

The action here is "identify and advance best practices". Is this a "federal decision"? It's a policy initiative.
The engagement is "to gather information".
In the Navy example, the consultation was for "financial analysis associated with the report". The label was No.
Here, the engagement is to "gather information regarding opportunities". This is very similar to the Navy example. It is information gathering for a study/initiative, not consultation on a specific regulatory or project decision.

Therefore, the label should be No.
